items.title: Ottermind (+Free Tier): This ALL-IN-ONE AI Agent is CRAZY GOOD!
items.summary:
Try Ottermind AI here: https://ottermind.ai/?utm_source=YT&utm_medium=DED-EN&utm_campaign=AICodeKing 

Discover how Ottermind AI helps you automate tasks, conduct AI-powered research, analyze files, generate reports, and complete real work with autonomous AI agents.

In this video, I'll be telling you about Ottermind AI, an AI-powered workspace built around autonomous AI agents that can turn messy inputs like PDFs, spreadsheets, notes, and prompts into finished deliverables such as presentations, reports, websites, images, and automated workflows.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Ottermind AI is an autonomous AI workspace designed to generate outcomes, not just answers.
🤖 It includes multiple built-in AI models like Ottermind Lite, Ottermind Pro, GPT-5.6 models, Claude models, and GLM-5.2 with no API key setup required.
📊 You can create slides, summarize files, generate images, analyze spreadsheets, and build websites from one simple prompt.
🎨 The Slides workflow supports Professional mod
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, over the past year, we've seen a bunch of these AI agent platforms pop up. You've got Manifold, ChatGPT agent, GenSpark, Perplexity Labs, OpenClaw, Hermes, and a whole lot more. The whole idea behind these is that instead of just chatting with an AI and getting a block of text back, you give it a goal and it actually goes and does the work for you. Today, we're looking at another player in this space called OtterMind AI. It's an AI-powered workspace built around autonomous AI agents, and the pitch is pretty simple. Most AI tools help you generate answers. OtterMind AI helps you generate outcomes. So, you can start with a messy input like a bunch of PDFs, a spreadsheet, some rough notes, or even just a single prompt, and it takes that through planning, execution, and then gives you an actual finished deliverable. That could be a report, a presentation, a website, images, an analysis, or even an automated workflow that runs on a schedule. So, it's less of a chatbot and more of an AI teammate that sits inside a workspace with your files, tasks, and outputs all connected together. I've been testing it out, and there are some things here that I quite like. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about what you see when you open it up. When you land on the home screen, you get a clean workspace with a prompt box in the middle that says, "What's on your mind today?" and a few action buttons underneath. So, it's not just asking you to chat, it's asking you what kind of work you want done. Now, the first thing I want to point out is the model selector in the upper left corner. This controls which AI model powers the main agent, and there are eight options in here. You get OtterMind Light, which is the free one for quick everyday tasks and fast responses. Then there's OtterMind Pro, which is their premium option for higher-quality outputs and complex tasks. And then, you get access to a bunch of frontier models as well. There's GPT 5.6 Soul, which is OpenAI's latest flagship for complex reasoning, GPT-5.6 Terra for fast web-aware tasks, and GPT-5.6 Luna, which is the creative one for writing and storytelling. On the Anthropic side, you get Claude Fable 5, which is their latest premium model for complex multi-step workflows, and Claude Sonnet 5 for advanced reasoning and planning. And there's also GLM-5.2 from Zhipu, which is really good for multilingual stuff. And here's the part I like. All of these are already built into OtterMind AI. There's no API key, no external setup, no configuration, nothing. You just pick a model from the drop-down and start working. Considering how many tools make you go create API keys on three different platforms and paste them in. This is pretty good, for sure. You'll also see your credit balance in the top right area, so you always know how much you have available for generation and testing. Now, below the prompt box, you get five main action buttons, and these are basically the fastest ways to start real work. You've got create slides, which turns a prompt or your source files into a presentation deck, summarize file, which reads an uploaded document and pulls out the key points, generate image, which creates images from text prompts, analyze spreadsheet, which reads your data and finds insights, trends, and issues, and build website, which creates an actual webpage from a prompt. So, the way I describe it is that OtterMind AI helps you create, understand, and transform work from one simple prompt. You don't just chat with it. You ask it to build, analyze, summarize, and create real outputs. Anyway, now let's actually test this thing, because talking about buttons is one thing and seeing the output is another. So, the first thing I'm testing is the slides workflow, because this is where OtterMind AI has a really interesting trick. When you click create slides, it automatically switches into slides mode. And here you get two ways to generate your presentation. The first option is professional mode, which uses AutoMind AI's built-in slide engine. This one is all about speed and clean structure. It's good for quick business presentations, internal reports, and simple decks, but the design is fairly minimal. So, if you want something fancy, you might have to edit it up a bit. The second option is the AI model selector, and this is the one you want for anything client-facing. Instead of the built-in engine, you can pick which image generation model creates the visuals for your slides. Right now, you can choose between Nano Banana and GPT Image 2. And again, no API keys, no external services, nothing to configure. It's all built in. I went with Nano Banana because it creates much richer slides with stronger graphics, illustrations, and overall better presentation aesthetics. So, for the test, I gave it a prompt to create a six-slide pitch deck for a new productivity app, and let's send it and see. Okay, so it plans out the deck first, then starts generating each slide one by one. And if we wait a bit, it's now done. And honestly, these look really good. You get an eye-catching AI-generated cover slide, and the visuals actually look designed rather than generated. The best part is that the presentation is fully editable. It's not just flattened into images, so you can go in and change the text afterwards. Compared to manually building an image-based PowerPoint, this is way faster. So, this is kind of great. Now, the same AI model selector also shows up in the generate image workflow. So, you click generate image, pick between Nano Banana and GPT Image 2, and just start creating. I generated a clean hero image for an AI productivity platform, and the composition and prompt understanding are quite solid. This is useful for thumbnails, marketing assets, social media graphics, product visuals, all of that. And depending on your account, there's also video generation, so you can do text-to-video and image-to-video workflows as well, which turns this into more of a full creative production workspace. Anyway, now let's come to the part that I think is actually the strongest use case, which is the multi-file workflow. So, instead of uploading one document, I threw a PDF report, a sales spreadsheet, and some rough meeting notes at it and asked it to read everything, extract the key insights, supporting data, risks, and recommendations, and create an executive presentation out of it. And this is where you can see that it's an actual agent and not just a text generator. It breaks the work into steps, shows you its progress as it reads and analyzes each file, plans the structure, and then moves through the workflow towards the final result. You can just let it run in the background and come back when it's done. And at the end, you get an actual file card in the workspace that you can open, review, share, or keep working on. That moment where you open the finished deck built from three messy files is honestly the whole pitch of this product in one shot. This normally takes hours of reading, organizing, and formatting, and it just happened while I was doing something else. And the first output is not the end, either. You can keep iterating on the deliverable through conversation. So, you can say, "Make this presentation more visual." or "Rewrite this report for executives." or "Improve the website copy and make the call to action clearer." And it just updates the deliverable. So, you can go from draft to polished result without starting over. Now, there are a few more features here that make it feel like a proper workspace instead of a chat window. First, everything stays organized in the workspace, so your files, generated outputs, and project context all live together instead of being buried in some chat history. Second, you get scheduled automations, so you can set up something like, "Every Monday at 9:00 a.m., generate a weekly summary of important AI agent news and trends." and it just runs on its own and produces the deliverable every week. You can do daily market summaries, weekly team reports, recurring research briefs, that kind of stuff. This is the part that separates it from one-time chat tools, and I think this is pretty amazing, to be honest. Third, it has reusable AI skills, which basically means it has specialized built-in abilities for different kinds of work like documents, spreadsheets, slides, PDFs, images, websites, and automation. That's why the outputs come out as real structured files instead of just plain text. And fourth, there's project memory. For longer projects, AutoMind AI keeps the context of what you're working on, so you don't have to repeat your goal, audience, tone, and preferences over and over. Follow-up work becomes way easier because of this. So, how does it compare to the other tools? Well, if you ask me, the simplest way to think about AutoMind AI is that it's like a combination of ChatGPT, Many of project management tools, file workflows, and automation tools inside a single AI workspace. ChatGPT helps you think, but AutoMind AI is built to get the work done and hand you the file at the end. And compared to something like Perplexity Labs, research is just the starting point here. Execution is the goal. It's not perfect, of course. The professional slides mode is a bit minimal, and as with any AI agent, you'll want to review the outputs before sending them to a client. But the core loop of messy input to polished output works really well, and the fact that all the models and image generators are built-in with zero setup makes it very easy to just start. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super [music] Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until [music] then, bye. >> [music] [bell]

items.title: Muse Glimmer 30B (Local Testing & Review): REALLY GOOD for LOCAL USAGE!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about Meta’s new open model called Muse Glimmer, a 30B local agentic model built for always-on workflows, reliable tool calling, multimodal vision, and local agent setups.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Meta has released Muse Glimmer, a new 30B open agentic model optimized for local workflows.
🛠️ The model is especially strong at tool calling, multi-step agent tasks, and recovering from failures.
📉 It does not perform very well on general benchmarks, so it is not meant to compete with top benchmark models.
🔗 Muse Glimmer works well with agentic tools like Hermes Agent, OpenCode, LM Studio, and local endpoints.
🖼️ The model is multimodal and includes a dedicated perception encoder for handling images alongside text.
💻 It can run locally with full context on a 48GB RAM Mac using 4-bit quantization.
⚠️ Since it is a dense 30B model and not an MoE, it requires more memory and may be difficult to run on 16GB or 24GB machines.
📜 Muse Glimmer is MIT licensed, making
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Meta has released a new open model called Muse Glimmer. This is a 30 billion parameter model that they are calling an open agentic model, and it's specifically optimized for always-on local agent workflows. Basically, it's a model that's made to sit on your machine and do agentic stuff like tool calling, multi-step reasoning, and recovering from failures without falling apart. Now, when this came out, I looked at it and I honestly didn't think it was worth testing on my benchmarks. It's a 30B local agent model, and these kinds of models are not really made for the type of questions that I test. But, I still went ahead and tested it anyway, just to see where it lands. And yeah, my instinct was right. The results weren't that good. None of them were really impressive. So, I didn't include it in my official records. There's no point in putting it on the leaderboard when the model was never trying to compete there in the first place. But, here's the thing. This model is really good at what it is actually made for, and that is tool calling. I hooked it up and ran it through some agentic workflows, and it works very reliably in tool calling. It doesn't mangle the tool call formats. It doesn't hallucinate random tools, and it picks the right tool at the right time. It just works. And honestly, that's more than I can say for a lot of bigger models. It works well with things like Hermes agent and other agentic setups. You can get it quite easily from LM Studio. And once you have it running there, you can plug it into things like Hermes, open code, and other tools that can talk to a local endpoint. So, if you want a local model that just sits there and reliably drives your agents, this is a really good option for sure. Another thing that's really great to see is that this model is multimodal. It has a dedicated perception encoder, so it can handle images along with text. And the vision capabilities are actually really good. I threw some images at it, and it was able to understand them properly, which is not something you usually get from local agentic models. Most of them are text-only, so having solid vision built into an agent model is quite great to see. Now, let's talk about running it locally. I was able to run it with the full context length via LM Studio on my Mac that has 48 gigs of RAM, and it worked really well and fast. With the 4-bit quantization, the memory usage stays manageable, and the generation speed was totally usable for agentic work. So, if you have a Mac with a decent amount of unified memory, you should be able to run this without any issues. But, there are still some issues with it. The main one is that this is not an OE model like Gemma 4. It's a dense 30B model, which means all the parameters are active all the time, and that requires a larger memory footprint as well. With an OE, you get faster inference and lower effective compute for the same kind of quality. So, a dense model at this size feels a bit dated in that sense. If you're on a machine with 16 or 24 gigs of RAM, this is going to be a tight fit. On the licensing side, though, there's actually good news. The model is MIT-licensed instead of their older Llama OSL-style licenses. So, no weird acceptable use policies, no naming requirements, none of that. You can just take it and use it however you want, which is just amazing. It's really nice to see Meta finally moving to a proper permissive license. So, where does this leave us? If you're looking for a model to top benchmarks, this is not it, and that's fine. But, if you want a local model that does reliable tool calling, has genuinely good vision, runs at full context on something like a 48 gig Mac, and comes with an MIT license, then Muse Glimmer is honestly one of the better options right now. It knows what it's for, and it does that thing well. I'll be using it in some of my local agent setups, and I'll let you know how that goes in future videos. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, [music] consider donating through the Super Thanks option, or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. [music] Until then, bye.
